title: Completeness of Home Blood Pressure Diaries During Routine Hypertension Follow-up
background:
Home blood pressure (BP) diaries are used during routine hypertension follow-up, but the presence of a completed diary does not establish that all scheduled entries were recorded. In this fictional proposal, earlier feasibility reports describe variability in diary completion and the need for clarification when entries are missing or unclear.1,2 Neither diary completeness nor recorded systolic blood pressure (SBP, mmHg) is evidence that a new treatment has been assigned.

There are limited descriptive data for the two participating sites over a six-week observation period. The planned study will collect one scheduled home diary entry per day on Days 1–42. The Day 14 telephone contact is for recording clarification requests; the final Day 42 review counts entries and summarizes the diary. The two contacts have different purposes and their activities should not be combined.3

Reviewing diary completeness may help improve future instructions, but no direct benefit is guaranteed and the study does not test a treatment effect.
objective: Describe completeness of home blood pressure diaries over six weeks of routine hypertension follow-up.
hypothesis: Diary completeness may differ over the six-week observation period; this is an exploratory expectation rather than an established result.
population: Adults receiving routine outpatient follow-up for hypertension.
exclusion: Unable to consent or to provide a paper or electronic diary.
primary: Percentage of scheduled diary entries completed
secondary: Mean recorded systolic blood pressure (SBP, mmHg)
Diary Days 1 through 42, summarized at Day 42
timeline: Enrollment: 2 months; participant follow-up: 42 days; analysis: 1 month.
compensation: Travel reimbursement of up to USD 15 for the final visit; no participation payment.

procedures: Count completed and scheduled diary entries
Summarize recorded systolic blood pressure in mmHg from the diary

analysis: Summarize diary completion percentages using N, mean, standard deviation, median, minimum and maximum. Summarize clarification requests using counts and percentages. Use participants as the analysis unit. Report missing observations without imputation; no hypothesis tests are planned. For the secondary BP summary, calculate each participant's mean recorded SBP (mmHg) over available diary entries on Days 1–42, then report N, mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum across participants. Report the number of contributing diary entries; this descriptive summary is not a treatment-effect test.
privacy: Use study IDs in the analysis file. Only the site investigator can access the identity link. Store files on the sponsor's access-restricted server for 5 years after closeout; publish aggregate results only.
forbidden: A new antihypertensive treatment is assigned
Participants receive a guaranteed therapeutic benefit
sample_justification: Forty participants with evaluable diary data are considered sufficient for a descriptive feasibility summary. Allowing for eight participants with unavailable final data, the planned enrollment is 48 subjects across two sites, not 40 subjects. This is a convenience sample; no power calculation or inferential treatment comparison is planned.
potential_benefit: Reviewing diary completeness may help improve future instructions, but no direct benefit is guaranteed and the study does not test a treatment effect.

title: Recorded Hand Function and Prospective Activity Reports After Routine Hand Therapy
background:
Routine hand-therapy records contain grip-strength measurements in kilograms (kg), while later limitations in everyday activities are usually described by patients. Historical strength and future activity reports refer to different observation periods and cannot be treated as measurements made at the same visit. Fictional methodological examples describe this distinction and the effect of missing historical records on paired summaries.1,2

This ambispective study combines the most recent grip-strength record in the eight weeks before enrollment with prospective questionnaires at Week 0 and Week 12. The study-specific activity limitation score ranges from 0 to 100; higher scores indicate greater reported limitation. It is not represented as a validated instrument. No research grip-strength measurement or change to routine therapy is planned.3

Combining existing records with future questionnaires may improve understanding of activity limitations, but does not establish a treatment benefit or guarantee improvement for participants.
objective: Describe recorded grip strength and subsequent activity limitations after routine hand therapy.
hypothesis: Recorded grip strength may be associated with later reported activity limitations; the association is not established.
population: Adults who completed routine hand therapy within the preceding 8 weeks.
exclusion: Unavailable therapy records or inability to complete the activity questionnaire.
primary: Study-specific activity limitation questionnaire score (0–100; higher is greater limitation)
secondary: Most recent therapy record within 8 weeks before enrollment
timeline: Review records from the 8 weeks before enrollment; enroll over 3 months; prospective follow-up lasts 12 weeks; analysis takes 1 month.
compensation: None; no participation payment or reimbursement.

procedures: Abstract recorded grip strength from the preceding 8 weeks

analysis: Summarize activity scores using medians and interquartile ranges and recorded grip strength using means and standard deviations. Describe the association using a scatter plot without inferential testing. Report available pairs and missing observations; no imputation is planned.
forbidden: Historical grip strength is measured again for research
The study changes the therapy regimen
The eight-week historical period is added to prospective participant follow-up
sample_justification: A descriptive target of 60 available historical-strength/follow-up-score pairs is planned. Enrollment will be 72 participants to allow for 12 incomplete pairs. The enrollment total is 72; the expected evaluable subset of 60 is not a second enrollment target. No inferential power calculation is proposed.
potential_benefit: Combining existing records with future questionnaires may improve understanding of activity limitations, but does not establish a treatment benefit or guarantee improvement for participants.

title: Turnaround Times of Final Radiology Reports in Existing Outpatient Records
background:
Final radiology report availability and examination completion are separate timestamps in the existing outpatient record. Their difference can be summarized in hours (h), but a missing final timestamp is not a turnaround of zero hours. Fictional audit-method examples describe the distinction between excluded records and reports taking more than 24 h.1,2

The three sites lack a combined description for examinations completed from 1 January through 31 March 2026. This study will abstract existing completion time, final-report availability time and site. The denominator for the percentage finalized within 24 hours will be eligible records with both timestamps, with exclusions reported separately. Each eligible examination is the analysis unit. No new imaging, research visit or participant questionnaire is planned.3

The findings may help the sites understand existing reporting processes. This record review provides no direct participant benefit and does not demonstrate that any process change improves care.
objective: Describe the interval between examination completion and final report availability in existing outpatient radiology records.
hypothesis: Report turnaround may vary across sites; this descriptive expectation is unproven.
unmet_need: The participating sites lack a combined description of report turnaround for the selected record period.
population: Existing records of adult outpatient radiology examinations completed from 1 January through 31 March 2026.
exclusion: Duplicate examination records or records lacking either required timestamp.
primary: Hours from examination completion to final report
Existing records dated 1 January through 31 March 2026
secondary: Percentage of reports available within 24 hours
Existing records dated 1 January through 31 March 2026
timeline: Existing record period: 1 January through 31 March 2026; abstraction: 6 weeks; analysis: 2 weeks. No new participant contacts.
assessments: Abstract examination completion time, final report availability time and site from existing records dated 1 January through 31 March 2026. No new measurements, visits, questionnaires or participant contact are planned.
analysis: Summarize turnaround hours using medians and interquartile ranges overall and by site. Report the proportion available within 24 hours with explicit denominators. Count exclusions for missing timestamps separately. No imputation or inferential testing is planned.
privacy: Site personnel remove names before transfer. Use a coded study ID and retain the identity link only at the originating site. Restrict the combined file to named analysts and retain it for 3 years after closeout. Publish aggregate summaries only.
forbidden: Participants must sign an ICF before abstraction
Retrospective exemption or consent waiver has already been granted
An ICF or PRS XML belongs to the required document set
sample_justification: The descriptive analysis targets 120 eligible examination records across three sites. Up to 150 existing records may be screened to allow for approximately 30 duplicate or incomplete records. The analysis target remains 120 eligible records; 150 is the screening pool and is not participant enrollment. No inferential power calculation is planned.
potential_benefit: The findings may help the sites understand existing reporting processes. This record review provides no direct participant benefit and does not demonstrate that any process change improves care.
references: Example A, Sample B. Examination and report timestamps in a fictional outpatient audit. Synthetic Research Methods. 2023;1:10-19. Fictional test reference; not a real publication.

title: Comfort Reports During Routine Use of a Skin Moisturizer
background:
Adults who already use a moisturizer recommended during routine care may describe comfort differently over time. A diary can capture those reports without assigning a product or establishing product effectiveness. Fictional feasibility reports discuss diary adherence and the distinction between an observed comfort score and a treatment effect.1,2

The study-specific comfort scale is 0–10, with 0 meaning no comfort and 10 meaning the greatest comfort on this scale; it is not described as a validated instrument. One score is planned each day on Days 1–28. At the final telephone contact, staff review the diary, count available entries and record adverse events. No blood collection, research skin procedure or product switch is planned.3

The diary may help characterize comfort during routine use, but the study cannot establish effectiveness or promise improvement or direct benefit.
objective: Describe daily comfort reports during four weeks of routine moisturizer use.
hypothesis: Daily comfort scores may vary during observation; improvement is not assumed.
population: Adults already using a moisturizer recommended by their usual clinician.
exclusion: Known allergy to the existing moisturizer or inability to complete the diary.
primary: Mean daily study-specific comfort score (0–10; higher is greater comfort)
timeline: Enrollment: 1 month; follow-up: 28 days; analysis: 2 weeks.
compensation: USD 20 after the final questionnaire; no travel reimbursement.

procedures: Review daily comfort diary for Days 1 through 28

analysis: Summarize participant mean daily comfort scores using N, median, minimum and maximum. Summarize completed diary entries using counts. State the number of available diary days for every participant. No imputation, treatment comparison or hypothesis testing is planned.
forbidden: A moisturizer is assigned by the study
sample_justification: Thirty participants with available diaries are considered adequate for a descriptive feasibility summary. Enrollment is increased to 36 to allow for six unavailable diaries. The planned sample size is 36 participants, not 30. No formal power calculation or treatment comparison is planned.
potential_benefit: The diary may help characterize comfort during routine use, but the study cannot establish effectiveness or promise improvement or direct benefit.
references: Example A, Sample B. Comfort diaries during existing moisturizer use. Synthetic Research Methods. 2023;1:10-19. Fictional test reference; not a real publication.

title: Historical Hearing Aid Use and Subsequent Communication Reports in Routine Follow-up
background:
Routine hearing-aid records may contain device-use summaries expressed as hours per day (h/day). Later communication difficulty reports describe a different outcome, and greater historical use alone does not establish a causal improvement in communication. Fictional methodological examples emphasize keeping historical use and later patient reports separate.1,2

This ambispective study abstracts the three months before enrollment and collects questionnaires at Month 0, Month 1 and Month 3 after enrollment. The study-specific communication difficulty score ranges from 0 to 10, with higher scores indicating more difficulty; no validated-instrument claim is made. The primary endpoint is the Month 3 score. Month 1 is secondary. Historical records do not extend prospective follow-up from three to six months. No device-setting change is performed by research staff.3

Combining prior records with future questionnaires may inform counseling, but does not establish that counseling or a device causes improvement. Participants may receive no direct benefit.
objective: Describe historical hearing aid use and subsequent self-reported communication difficulty.
hypothesis: Historical hearing aid use may be associated with later communication reports; a causal effect is not established.
population: Adults with routine hearing aid records covering the 3 months before enrollment.
exclusion: Unavailable prior records or inability to complete the communication questionnaire.
primary: Study-specific communication difficulty questionnaire score (0–10; higher is greater difficulty)
secondary: Recorded hours of hearing aid use per day (h/day)
Study-specific communication difficulty questionnaire score (0–10; higher is greater difficulty)
timeline: Historical records cover 3 months before enrollment. Enrollment lasts 2 months, prospective follow-up lasts 3 months, and analysis lasts 1 month.
compensation: Travel reimbursement up to USD 25 per in-person follow-up; no participation payment.

procedures: Abstract prior 3 months of hearing aid use

analysis: Summarize communication scores and historical use using means, standard deviations, medians and ranges. Report available paired observations descriptively and identify missing questionnaires without imputation. No causal comparison or inferential testing is planned.
privacy: Use coded study IDs. Store the identity link separately at each site with investigator-only access. Retain study files for 7 years after closeout on an access-controlled server. Disclose identifiable records only to authorized study monitors and oversight bodies as permitted; publications use aggregate results.
forbidden: Three historical months extend prospective follow-up to six months
Hearing aid settings are changed by research staff
Questionnaire responses prove a causal benefit
sample_justification: The descriptive target is 56 participants with paired historical-use and Month 3 questionnaire data. Enrollment is 64 to allow for eight incomplete pairs. The enrollment total is 64, while 56 is the anticipated evaluable subset. No formal inferential power calculation is planned.
potential_benefit: Combining prior records with future questionnaires may inform counseling, but does not establish that counseling or a device causes improvement. Participants may receive no direct benefit.
